status: Fictional timed conversations for the cue timing simulation. Labels written on 14 November 2026 by the lab lane, before any evaluator was run on them, and awaiting the owner's review.
authorship: Written for people who work in software, AI and hiring. The author had read the three case sets, the phrase rules as described in docs/cue-intelligence.md, and an anonymized, abstracted description of how real meeting transcripts flow (turn lengths, backchannels, restatements, and which kinds of moment the conversation settles by itself). No real wording, name, organization or scenario is used.
format: atMs is when the speaker finishes the line, from the start of the call. expect is what should happen once that line has been heard: quiet (nothing changes); show (a cue about this line would help, described in about, with cue as words short enough for a card: at most ten; until names the line after which it no longer would, and without until it stays useful for the 18 seconds a cue lives); resolved or withdraw (this line answers, or removes the basis of, the cue for the line named in of); null (unlabelled: the note says why either choice is defensible). listener is the person TalkQTE would be helping. Labels are never sent to an evaluator.

conversations.title: Incident review

lines.speaker: Dana
lines.text: So timeline first. Alerts fired at ten past two, Kofi acked at two fourteen, and we rolled back at, what was it, two forty?

lines.speaker: Kofi
lines.text: Two thirty-eight. The rollback itself took about six minutes because the cache had to warm.

lines.speaker: Dana
lines.text: Okay, two thirty-eight. So roughly half an hour of failed logins.

lines.text: We had forty-one tickets in that window, and I told customers we'd publish a write-up.

lines.speaker: Dana
lines.text: Right, the write-up. That needs to go out at some point this week.

lines.speaker: Kofi
lines.text: Yeah, for sure.

lines.speaker: Dana
lines.text: And the bigger one is the alert threshold, because it was set at five percent and we sat at four point something for ten minutes before it tripped. Do we lower it, or add a second alert on latency?

lines.text: I'd add the latency one. Lowering it just pages us more, you know?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: I can take the write-up. I'll have a draft to Yuki by Wednesday.

lines.speaker: Dana
lines.text: Thanks Sam. Okay, let's not solve the threshold now, I'll put it on Thursday's ops agenda.

lines.speaker: Kofi
lines.text: Mm-hm.

lines.speaker: Dana

conversations.title: System design interview
conversations.setting: A technical interview. Amara is the candidate; a second interviewer is shadowing.

lines.speaker: Greg
lines.text: Thanks for joining, Amara. Can you hear us okay? Ilse is shadowing today, she'll mostly listen.

lines.speaker: Amara
lines.text: Yes, I can hear you fine.

lines.speaker: Greg
lines.text: Great. So here's the problem. Design a service that shortens links for an internal tool. Assume about five hundred writes a second, reads are a hundred times that, and links have to keep working for five years.
lines.about: The constraints, said once: five hundred writes a second, a hundred times as many reads, links kept for five years.
lines.cue: 500 writes a second, 100× reads, five years.

lines.speaker: Amara
lines.text: Okay. Can I ask a couple of clarifying questions first?

lines.speaker: Greg
lines.text: Of course.

lines.speaker: Amara
lines.text: Do the short links need to be guessable or not, and is there one region or several?

lines.speaker: Greg
lines.text: Not guessable, they can point at private documents. So think about how you'd generate the IDs.
lines.about: The second question, one region or several, was not answered.
lines.cue: Unanswered: one region or several?

lines.speaker: Amara
lines.text: Right. So I'd start with a random ID rather than a counter, maybe seven characters from a sixty-two character alphabet, and check for a collision on write.

lines.speaker: Greg
lines.text: Mm-hm. And how many links is that over the five years, roughly?
lines.note: A question to the candidate with no name in it. With one speaker label the evaluator cannot tell who is asked.

lines.speaker: Amara
lines.text: Five hundred a second is about forty-three million a day, so somewhere around eighty billion over five years.

lines.speaker: Greg
lines.text: Okay, good. Now two things. How would you handle a hot link that suddenly gets a million reads a minute, and, separately, what happens to a link when the person who made it leaves the company?
lines.about: Two questions: a hot link with a million reads a minute, and what happens to a link when its creator leaves.
lines.cue: Two parts: the hot link, and departed creators' links.

lines.speaker: Amara
lines.text: For the hot link I'd put a cache in front, keyed by the short ID, with a short expiry so a deleted link disappears quickly.

lines.speaker: Greg
lines.text: Makes sense. We've got about ten minutes left, so let me ask about storage.

lines.speaker: Ilse
lines.text: Sorry to jump in. Amara, you mentioned seven characters earlier, is that enough for eighty billion?
lines.about: Ilse asked Amara whether seven characters are enough for eighty billion links.
lines.cue: Asked you: are seven characters enough for eighty billion?

lines.speaker: Amara
lines.text: Sixty-two to the seventh is about three and a half trillion, so yes, with room to spare.
